annotations.keyFindings: Sensitivity for urgent messages 86 percent (95 percent CI 79 to 91), specificity 91 percent, prevalence 4 percent; sensitivity 71 percent for messages in languages other than English.
Each additional 10 messages per day was associated with 23 minutes more after-hours record work.
Two clinicians agreed moderately on same-day urgency (kappa 0.62); adjudication was needed for 14 percent of messages.
Across 12 studies sensitivity ranged from 62 to 94 percent; high risk of bias in reference standards; only 2 multi-site studies.
24 clinicians described after-hours work and fear of missing urgent messages; they wanted to know the miss rate before relying on a flag.
Messages from patients over 75 more often combined several requests; messages in languages other than English were three times as likely to be misrouted.
Sensitivity varied from 74 to 90 percent across five clinics, lowest where most messages were in languages other than English.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A validation study and a five-clinic study report sensitivity for urgent messages in the 74 to 90 percent range, lower for messages in languages other than English, and a review of 12 studies finds reference standards at high risk of bias and few multi-site studies. Clinician agreement on urgency is only moderate without adjudication. Message volume is linked to after-hours work, and clinicians want the miss rate before relying on a flag. A multi-site study with an adjudicated reference standard, random sampling and results by clinic and language is needed.
gradeRationale: Few accuracy studies, variable by population, with frequent reference standard bias; workload evidence observational.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims; certainty low. One annotation carried an out-of-range relevance.
